title: Why music sends shivers down the spine
text: There is a moment {{1}} the chorus lifts, the strings rise and the hair on your arms stands up. Scientists call {{2}} happens 'frisson', and it is essentially a fight-or-flight response misfired by beauty: the brain braces {{3}} for a great event and then finds only sound. Brain scans {{4}} shown that music triggers the same reward circuitry as food and warmth, {{5}} explains why a favourite chorus still delivers after the hundredth hearing. The chills tend to arrive {{6}} a pattern is set up and then beautifully broken — an unexpected chord, a suspended note — {{7}} is why composers have exploited the trick for centuries. {{8}} sad music, of all things, should feel so good remains only partly understood, but for most listeners the shiver is its own explanation.

gaps.explanation: 'When' refers back to the moment in time.

gaps.explanation: 'Brace itself' — the brain prepares its own body.

gaps.explanation: Time clause: the chills arrive when the pattern breaks.
